910.name: Indigenous Peoples of Liamuiga and Oualie
910.description: The pre-Columbian indigenous civilizations of Saint Kitts (Liamuiga, 'fertile land') and Nevis (Oualie, 'land of beautiful waters'), from early Ciboney and Arawak settlements through the Kalinago (Island Carib) communities who inhabited the islands at the time of European contact.

sub_clusters.name: Ciboney and Arawak Settlement
sub_clusters.description: The earliest inhabitants, including Ciboney and later Arawak peoples, who migrated from South America through the island chain and established agricultural communities on both Saint Kitts and Nevis.

sub_clusters.name: Kalinago (Carib) Dominance
sub_clusters.description: The Kalinago (Island Caribs) displaced or absorbed earlier Arawak populations and established warrior communities on both islands. They named Saint Kitts 'Liamuiga' (fertile land) and Nevis 'Oualie' (land of beautiful waters). The Kalinago fiercely resisted European colonization for over a century.
key_events: Kalinago establish dominance over Liamuiga and Oualie by c. 1300

920.name: European Contact and the Mother Colony of the West Indies
920.description: Columbus's sighting of the islands, the establishment of both the first English and first French Caribbean colonies on Saint Kitts, the Kalinago massacre, and the early colonial rivalry that made Saint Kitts the 'Mother Colony' of English and French colonization in the Caribbean.

sub_clusters.name: Columbus's Sighting and Early Exploration
sub_clusters.description: Columbus sighted the islands on his second voyage in 1493, naming the larger island San Cristóbal (later Saint Christopher/Saint Kitts) and the smaller Nieves (Nevis, 'snows,' for its cloud-covered peak). For over a century, the islands remained under Kalinago control despite intermittent European visits.

sub_clusters.name: First English and French Colonies
sub_clusters.description: Sir Thomas Warner established the first English Caribbean colony on Saint Kitts in 1623, followed by Pierre Belain d'Esnambuc's French colony in 1625. The two nations initially cooperated, jointly massacring the indigenous Kalinago at Bloody Point in 1626 to eliminate resistance, then divided the island between them while using it as a base to colonize other islands.
key_events: Thomas Warner founds first English Caribbean colony on Saint Kitts — 1623
Pierre Belain d'Esnambuc founds first French Caribbean colony on Saint Kitts — 1625

930.name: Sugar, Slavery, and Anglo-French Colonial Wars
930.description: The transformation of both islands into sugar monocultures dependent on enslaved African labor, the repeated Anglo-French wars for control of Saint Kitts, and the strategic importance of Brimstone Hill fortress — the 'Gibraltar of the West Indies.'

sub_clusters.name: Sugar Economy and Enslaved Labor
sub_clusters.description: Both Saint Kitts and Nevis were transformed into sugar monocultures. Nevis became one of the wealthiest islands per capita in the Caribbean by the late 17th century. Tens of thousands of enslaved Africans were imported to work under brutal conditions on sugar plantations across both islands.

sub_clusters.name: Anglo-French Wars and Brimstone Hill Fortress
sub_clusters.description: Saint Kitts was contested between England and France in multiple wars. The French captured the island in 1666, 1689, and briefly in 1782 after a siege of Brimstone Hill fortress. The Treaty of Versailles (1783) permanently ceded the entire island to Britain. Brimstone Hill, now a UNESCO World Heritage Site, earned the name 'Gibraltar of the West Indies.'
key_events: Siege of Brimstone Hill and French capture 1782
Treaty of Versailles confirms British sovereignty over Saint Kitts 1783

sub_clusters.name: Nevis Plantation Society
sub_clusters.description: Nevis developed its own distinctive plantation society, becoming fabulously wealthy in the late 1600s. It was the birthplace of Alexander Hamilton (1755/1757) and the marriage place of Horatio Nelson (1787). Sugar monoculture eventually exhausted Nevis's soil, leading to economic decline.
key_events: Alexander Hamilton born on Nevis c. 1755
Horatio Nelson marries Fanny Nisbet on Nevis 1787

940.name: Emancipation and Economic Decline
940.description: The abolition of the slave trade, emancipation in 1834, the difficult transition to free labor, and the long economic decline as sugar prices collapsed and both islands struggled to adapt to the post-slavery economy.

sub_clusters.name: Abolition and Emancipation
sub_clusters.description: The abolition of the slave trade (1807) and the Emancipation Act (1834) freed the enslaved populations of Saint Kitts and Nevis, though an apprenticeship period delayed full freedom until 1838. The freed population faced limited economic options as planters retained ownership of nearly all arable land.

sub_clusters.name: Post-Emancipation Sugar Decline
sub_clusters.description: Both islands experienced severe economic decline as sugar prices fell due to competition from beet sugar and larger producers. The planter class maintained social control but faced mounting debts. Workers endured poverty and limited political rights under the Crown Colony system.

950.name: Labour Movement and Path to Independence
950.description: The emergence of the labour movement under Robert Bradshaw, the sugar workers' struggles, the West Indies Federation experiment, associated statehood, and the long negotiations leading to independence in 1983 — making Saint Kitts and Nevis the smallest sovereign state in the Americas.

sub_clusters.name: Sugar Workers and the Labour Movement
sub_clusters.description: The sugar industry continued to dominate both islands' economies into the 20th century. The 1935 sugar workers' strike was a watershed moment, and Robert Llewellyn Bradshaw emerged as the labor movement's leader, founding the St. Kitts-Nevis Trades and Labour Union and later the Labour Party.
key_events: 1935 sugar workers' strike on Saint Kitts
Robert Bradshaw leads the labour movement from the 1940s

sub_clusters.name: Federation, Associated Statehood, and Bradshaw Era
sub_clusters.description: Saint Kitts-Nevis-Anguilla gained universal suffrage in 1952 and joined the West Indies Federation (1958–1962). Under Bradshaw as Chief Minister and then Premier, the islands became an associated state in 1967. Anguilla rebelled against Kittitian rule and separated in 1971. Bradshaw dominated politics until his death in 1978.

sub_clusters.name: Independence in 1983
sub_clusters.description: After Bradshaw's death and protracted negotiations — complicated by Nevis's desire for a loose federation — Saint Kitts and Nevis achieved independence on September 19, 1983, under Prime Minister Kennedy Simmonds of the People's Action Movement. The constitution gave Nevis considerable autonomy, including the right to secede.
key_events: Independence of Saint Kitts and Nevis — September 19, 1983
Kennedy Simmonds becomes first Prime Minister

960.name: Contemporary Saint Kitts and Nevis
960.description: Post-independence challenges and innovations: the closure of the centuries-old sugar industry, the Nevis secession referendum, the pioneering citizenship-by-investment program, tourism development, and the smallest nation in the Americas navigating climate change and economic diversification.

sub_clusters.name: Nevis Secession Referendum
sub_clusters.description: Long-simmering Nevisian desires for independence from Saint Kitts culminated in a secession referendum on August 10, 1998. The vote favored secession 61.7% to 38.3%, but fell short of the required two-thirds supermajority. Tensions between the islands have continued intermittently.

sub_clusters.name: Closure of the Sugar Industry
sub_clusters.description: After over 350 years of sugar production, the government closed the state-owned sugar company in 2005 due to persistent losses and the end of EU preferential pricing. The closure marked the end of an era that had defined the islands' identity, economy, and social structure since the 1640s.
key_events: Closure of the sugar industry — July 2005 — ending 350+ years of production

sub_clusters.name: Citizenship-by-Investment and Economic Diversification
sub_clusters.description: Saint Kitts and Nevis launched the world's first citizenship-by-investment program in 1984, which became a major revenue source. The economy diversified into tourism, financial services, and real estate development, though vulnerability to hurricanes and climate change remains a significant challenge.
key_events: Tourism surpasses sugar as primary economic driver by 2000s
